title: "Hadoop Ecosystem Usage Guide"
format: html
---

This guide provides usage instructions and examples for various tools integrated into our Hadoop environment. It covers all 36 components of the deployed stack.

## Apache Hadoop

Apache Hadoop is an open-source framework for distributed storage and processing of large datasets on clusters of commodity hardware. It consists of the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) for storage, and Yet Another Resource Negotiator (YARN) for job scheduling and cluster resource management. Hadoop's fault-tolerant and scalable architecture makes it the foundation of the modern big data ecosystem.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Master Nodes"
        NameNode["NameNode (Metadata)"]
        ResourceManager["ResourceManager (Job Scheduler)"]
    end
    subgraph "Worker Nodes"
        direction LR
        DataNode1["DataNode (Block Storage)"]
        NodeManager1["NodeManager (Task Runner)"]
        DataNode2["DataNode (Block Storage)"]
        NodeManager2["NodeManager (Task Runner)"]
        DataNode3["DataNode (Block Storage)"]
        NodeManager3["NodeManager (Task Runner)"]
    end
    NameNode -- Manages --> DataNode1
    NameNode -- Manages --> DataNode2
    NameNode -- Manages --> DataNode3
    ResourceManager -- Manages --> NodeManager1
    ResourceManager -- Manages --> NodeManager2
    ResourceManager -- Manages --> NodeManager3
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Large File] --> B{Client splits into Blocks};
    B --> C[Block 1];
    B --> D[Block 2];
    C -- Replicated to --> E[DataNode 1];
    C -- Replicated to --> F[DataNode 2];
    D -- Replicated to --> G[DataNode 2];
    D -- Replicated to --> H[DataNode 3];
```

### Examples (HDFS Command Line)

1.  **List Files**: List the contents of the HDFS root directory.
    ```bash
    hdfs dfs -ls /
    ```
2.  **Create a Directory**: Make a new directory for a user.
    ```bash
    hdfs dfs -mkdir -p /user/alice
    ```
3.  **Copy a File to HDFS**: Upload a local file to the new directory.
    ```bash
    hdfs dfs -put local_data.csv /user/alice/
    ```
4.  **Read a File from HDFS**: Display the contents of a file stored in HDFS.
    ```bash
    hdfs dfs -cat /user/alice/local_data.csv
    ```
5.  **Check Cluster Health**: Get a report on the status of the HDFS cluster.
    ```bash
    hdfs dfsadmin -report
    ```

## Apache Spark

Apache Spark is a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing, with built-in modules for SQL, streaming, machine learning, and graph processing. It is known for its speed, which is achieved by performing computations in-memory, and its ease of use through rich APIs in Scala, Java, Python, and R. Spark integrates seamlessly with Hadoop, using YARN for resource management and HDFS for storage.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "User Applications"
        A[Spark SQL]
        B[DataFrame API]
        C[Streaming]
        D[MLlib]
    end
    subgraph "Spark Core Engine"
        E[Driver Program] --> F{SparkContext};
        F -- Manages --> G[Cluster Manager YARN];
        G -- Acquires --> H[Executors on Worker Nodes];
    end
    A & B & C & D --> E
    H -- Reads/Writes Data --> I[HDFS];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Driver] -- "Creates logical plan (DAG)" --> B(DAG Scheduler);
    B -- "Splits into stages/tasks" --> C(Task Scheduler);
    C -- "Launches tasks on executors" --> D{Executor 1};
    C -- "Launches tasks on executors" --> E{Executor 2};
    D -- "Executes task" --> F[Result];
    E -- "Executes task" --> G[Result];
```

### Examples

1.  **Interactive Shell (PySpark)**: Read a file from HDFS and count the lines.
    ```python
    # Run 'pyspark' from the command line
    df = spark.read.text("hdfs:///user/alice/local_data.csv")
    print(df.count())
    ```
2.  **DataFrame Operations (Python)**: Perform a simple transformation and filter.
    ```python
    df.select(df['value'].alias('line')).filter("line LIKE '%error%'").show()
    ```
3.  **Spark SQL**: Register a DataFrame as a temporary view and query it with SQL.
    ```python
    df.createOrReplaceTempView("logs")
    errors = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM logs WHERE value LIKE '%error%'")
    errors.show()
    ```
4.  **Submit a Python Script**: Run a standalone application on the cluster.
    ```bash
    /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit \
      --master yarn \
      --deploy-mode cluster \
      my_spark_app.py
    ```
5.  **Write Data to HDFS**: Save the results of a transformation back to HDFS as Parquet.
    ```python
    errors.write.parquet("hdfs:///user/alice/error_logs")
    ```

## Apache Druid

Apache Druid is a real-time analytics database designed for fast slice-and-dice queries on large, streaming datasets. It uses a columnar, time-series oriented architecture to power interactive applications and dashboards where low-latency query performance is critical. Druid decouples its storage from its compute, using a "deep storage" layer like HDFS for permanent data archival.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Streaming Data (Kafka)<br/>Batch Data (HDFS)] --> B{Druid Ingestion<br/>(Indexer)};
    B --> C[Druid Segments<br/>(Time-chunked, columnar)];
    C -- Published to --> D[(Deep Storage - HDFS)];
    D -- Loaded by --> E[Historical Nodes];
    F[Real-time Nodes] -- Ingests --> A;
    G[SQL / API Query] --> H{Broker Node};
    H -- Queries --> E;
    H -- Queries --> F;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph Query Path
        User -- SQL --> Broker
    end
    subgraph Data Nodes
        Broker -- Scatter/Gather --> Historicals
        Broker -- Scatter/Gather --> MiddleManagers
    end
    subgraph External Dependencies
        direction TB
        Historicals -- Loads Segments from --> DeepStorage[(HDFS)]
        Broker & Historicals & MiddleManagers -- Use for Metadata --> ZK[(ZooKeeper)]
    end
```

### Examples

1.  **Batch Ingestion Spec (JSON)**: A task to load data from HDFS.
    ```json
    {
      "type": "index_parallel",
      "spec": {
        "ioConfig": { "type": "index_parallel", "inputSource": { "type": "hdfs", "paths": "hdfs:///path/to/data/" }},
        "dataSchema": { "dataSource": "my_data", "parser": { "type": "string", "parseSpec": { "format": "json", "dimensionsSpec": { "dimensions": ["product", "country"] }, "timestampSpec": { "column": "ts", "format": "auto" }}}},
        "tuningConfig": { "type": "index_parallel" }
      }
    }
    ```
2.  **SQL Query - Count Total Events**:
    ```sql
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM my_data WHERE __time >= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' DAY;
    ```
3.  **SQL Query - Group By**: Find the top 5 products by page views.
    ```sql
    SELECT page, COUNT(*) AS views
    FROM my_data
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY 2 DESC
    LIMIT 5;
    ```
4.  **SQL Query - Time Series**: Get the number of events per hour.
    ```sql
    SELECT TIME_FLOOR(__time, 'PT1H') AS hour, COUNT(*)
    FROM my_data
    GROUP BY 1;
    ```
5.  **SQL Query - Approximate Distinct Count**:
    ```sql
    SELECT APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(userId) FROM my_data;
    ```

## Apache Beam

Apache Beam provides a unified, open-source programming model for defining both batch and streaming data processing pipelines. You write your pipeline once using one of the Beam SDKs (like Java or Python) and then choose a distributed processing back-end, or "Runner," to execute it. This allows for portable pipelines that can run on various engines like Spark, Flink, or Google Cloud Dataflow without rewriting the core logic.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Your Python/Java Code] -- Beam SDK --> B{Portable Pipeline};
    B -- Executes On --> C[Beam Runner];
    subgraph "Choose a Runner"
        C --- D[Spark Runner]
        C --- E[Flink Runner]
        C --- F[Dataflow Runner]
    end
    D -- Runs on --> G{{YARN Cluster}};
```

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[PCollection] -- "Represents a dataset" --> B(Pipeline);
    subgraph "Inside a Beam Pipeline"
        B -- "Apply Transform" --> C["PTransform (e.g., Map)"];
        C --> D[PCollection];
        D -- "Apply Transform" --> E["PTransform (e.g., GroupBy)"];
        E --> F[PCollection];
    end
```

### Examples

1.  **Word Count (Python)**: A classic batch processing example.
    ```python
    import apache_beam as beam
    from apache_beam.options.pipeline_options import PipelineOptions

    options = PipelineOptions(runner='SparkRunner')
    with beam.Pipeline(options=options) as p:
        (p | 'Read' >> beam.io.ReadFromText('hdfs:///user/data/input.txt')
           | 'Split' >> beam.FlatMap(lambda x: x.split())
           | 'Count' >> beam.combiners.Count.PerElement()
           | 'Write' >> beam.io.WriteToText('hdfs:///user/data/output'))
    ```
2.  **Filtering Data**: Keep only lines containing a specific word.
    ```python
    lines | 'Filter' >> beam.Filter(lambda line: 'ERROR' in line)
    ```
3.  **Applying a Schema**: Convert raw data into structured `Row` objects.
    ```python
    lines | 'ToRow' >> beam.Map(lambda x: beam.Row(word=x, length=len(x)))
    ```
4.  **Grouping Data**: Group words by their first letter.
    ```python
    words | 'GroupByInitial' >> beam.GroupBy(lambda word: word[0])
    ```
5.  **Streaming Pipeline**: Read from a streaming source like Kafka (conceptual).
    ```python
    (p | 'ReadFromKafka' >> beam.io.kafka.ReadFromKafka(...)
       | 'Windowing' >> beam.WindowInto(beam.window.FixedWindows(60))
       | 'Process' >> ...)
    ```
## Apache BookKeeper

Apache BookKeeper is a scalable, fault-tolerant, and low-latency storage service optimized for real-time workloads. It is often used as a replicated log store, providing a durable foundation for messaging systems like Apache Pulsar or for storing state in streaming applications. BookKeeper achieves high throughput by separating the journal (for fast writes) from the ledger storage (for long-term persistence).

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Client Application"
        Client --> WriteRequest["Write(data)"];
    end
    subgraph "BookKeeper Cluster"
        WriteRequest --> B1[Bookie 1];
        WriteRequest --> B2[Bookie 2];
        WriteRequest --> B3[Bookie 3];
        B1 -- "Ack" --> Client;
        B2 -- "Ack" --> Client;
        B3 -- "Ack" --> Client;
    end
    subgraph "Coordination"
        Client -- "Reads/writes metadata" --> ZK[(ZooKeeper)];
        B1 & B2 & B3 -- "Register/discover" --> ZK;
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Client Write] --> B{Journal (on SSD)};
    B -- "Flushed periodically" --> C{Ledger Storage (on HDD)};
    D[Client Read] --> E{Read Cache};
    E -- "Cache Miss" --> C;
```

### Examples

1.  **Create a Ledger (Java API)**: The basic unit of storage in BookKeeper is a ledger.
    ```java
    // Assumes 'bkc' is a connected BookKeeper client
    LedgerHandle lh = bkc.createLedger(3, 3, BookKeeper.DigestType.MAC, "password".getBytes());
    ```
2.  **Add Entries to a Ledger (Java API)**: Write data sequentially to the created ledger.
    ```java
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
        lh.addEntry(("entry-" + i).getBytes());
    }
    ```
3.  **Read Entries from a Ledger (Java API)**: Read a range of entries from the ledger.
    ```java
    Enumeration<LedgerEntry> entries = lh.readEntries(0, 99);
    while(entries.hasMoreElements()) {
        LedgerEntry entry = entries.nextElement();
        // process entry.getEntry()
    }
    ```
4.  **Close a Ledger (Java API)**: Close the ledger once you are finished writing to it.
    ```java
    lh.close();
    ```
5.  **Check Cluster Status (CLI)**: Use the command-line tool to inspect the cluster's health.
    ```bash
    /opt/bookkeeper/bin/bookkeeper shell bookiesanity
    ```

## Apache CarbonData

Apache CarbonData is a columnar storage format designed for fast analytics on big data platforms like Apache Spark. It integrates several advanced features, including indexing, compression, and a columnar layout, to accelerate query performance significantly. CarbonData is not a standalone service but a library that plugs into a query engine, providing an efficient way to store and query large datasets.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Spark SQL Query] --> B{Spark Engine};
    B -- "Reads data from" --> C[CarbonData Files];
    subgraph "Inside CarbonData File"
        C --> D[Blocklet];
        D --> E[Columnar Data Chunks];
        D --> F[Indexes];
    end
    F -- "Prunes blocklets" --> B;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Raw Data] --> B{Spark DataFrame};
    B -- "df.write.format(\"carbondata\")" --> C[CarbonData Files on HDFS];
    subgraph "File Structure"
        C --> D[Fact File (.carbon)];
        C --> E[Index File (.carbonindex)];
    end
```

### Examples (Spark SQL)

1.  **Create a CarbonData Table**: Use SQL DDL to create a table using the CarbonData format.
    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE sales(
        id INT,
        product STRING,
        amount DECIMAL
    )
    STORED AS carbondata;
    ```
2.  **Load Data into a Table**: Insert data from another table or a file.
    ```sql
    LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH '/path/to/sales.csv' INTO TABLE sales;
    ```
3.  **Query Data**: Run a standard SQL query. Spark will use CarbonData's indexes to speed it up.
    ```sql
    SELECT product, SUM(amount)
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY product;
    ```
4.  **Create an Index**: Build a secondary index on a column to further accelerate filtering.
    ```sql
    CREATE INDEX idx_product ON TABLE sales (product) AS 'carbondata';
    ```
5.  **Update Data**: CarbonData supports UPDATE and DELETE operations, which are uncommon for analytical formats.
    ```sql
    UPDATE sales SET amount = amount * 1.1 WHERE product = 'Laptop';
    ```

## Apache Calcite

Apache Calcite is a dynamic data management framework that provides powerful SQL parsing, validation, and optimization capabilities. It is not a database itself but a library that other systems can use to add standard SQL support and advanced query optimization. Calcite allows developers to build databases and data processing engines without having to implement a complex query planner from scratch.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[SQL Query] --> B{Calcite SQL Parser};
    B --> C[Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)];
    C --> D{AST Validator};
    D --> E[Relational Algebra Expression];
    E --> F{Query Optimizer};
    F -- "Applies rules" --> G[Optimized Relational Expression];
    G --> H[Executable Plan];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Your Application"
        A[Data Source Adapter]
        B[Calcite Core Engine]
        C[Query Processor]
    end
    D[SQL Query] --> B;
    B -- "Gets schema from" --> A;
    B -- "Generates plan for" --> C;
```

### Examples (Java API)

1.  **Parsing a SQL Query**: Convert a SQL string into a parsed tree.
    ```java
    SqlParser.Config config = SqlParser.config().withLex(Lex.MYSQL);
    SqlParser parser = SqlParser.create("SELECT * FROM emps", config);
    SqlNode sqlNode = parser.parseQuery();
    ```
2.  **Validating a Query**: Check the parsed query against a schema.
    ```java
    // Requires a configured CalciteConnection and validator
    SqlValidator validator = ...;
    SqlNode validatedNode = validator.validate(sqlNode);
    ```
3.  **Creating a Relational Expression**: Convert the validated node into a logical plan.
    ```java
    // Requires a configured Planner
    Planner planner = Frameworks.getPlanner(config);
    RelRoot relRoot = planner.rel(validatedNode);
    RelNode logicalPlan = relRoot.project();
    ```
4.  **Optimizing a Plan**: Apply a set of rules to transform the logical plan into an efficient physical plan.
    ```java
    // HepPlanner is one of Calcite's optimizers
    HepProgram program = new HepProgramBuilder().addRuleInstance(MyRule.INSTANCE).build();
    HepPlanner hepPlanner = new HepPlanner(program);
    hepPlanner.setRoot(logicalPlan);
    RelNode optimizedPlan = hepPlanner.findBestExp();
    ```
5.  **Building a Schema Adapter**: Implement the `SchemaFactory` interface to teach Calcite about your custom data source.
    ```java
    public class MySchemaFactory implements SchemaFactory {
      public Schema create(SchemaPlus parentSchema, String name, Map<String, Object> operand) {
        // Return a new instance of your custom schema
        return new MyCustomSchema();
      }
    }
    ```

## Apache Daffodil

Apache Daffodil is an open-source implementation of the Data Format Description Language (DFDL), which is used to parse complex data formats into an information set. It is particularly useful for parsing fixed-format textual and binary data, such as legacy scientific formats, EDI, or financial data feeds. Daffodil can be used as a command-line tool or as a library within a larger application.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Raw Data (Binary/Text)] --> B{Daffodil Parser};
    C[DFDL Schema (.dfdl.xsd)] -- "Defines the data structure" --> B;
    B -- "Produces" --> D[Infoset (XML/JSON)];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[DFDL Schema] -- "Defines" --> B(Data Elements);
    B -- "Have properties like" --> C{Type: String, Int};
    B -- "Have properties like" --> D{Length: Fixed, Delimited};
    B -- "Have properties like" --> E{Encoding: ASCII, EBCDIC};
```

### Examples

1.  **Create a DFDL Schema**: A simple schema for a comma-separated list of numbers.
    ```xml
    <xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:dfdl="http://www.ogf.org/dfdl/dfdl-1.0/">
      <xs:element name="numbers">
        <xs:complexType>
          <xs:sequence dfdl:separator=",">
            <xs:element name="num" type="xs:int" dfdl:lengthKind="delimited" maxOccurs="unbounded" />
          </xs:sequence>
        </xs:complexType>
      </xs:element>
    </xs:schema>
    ```
2.  **Parse Data (CLI)**: Use the Daffodil CLI to parse a data file against the schema.
    ```bash
    daffodil parse --schema my_schema.dfdl.xsd --output result.xml my_data.txt
    ```
3.  **Unparse Data (CLI)**: Convert an XML infoset back into its native format.
    ```bash
    daffodil unparse --schema my_schema.dfdl.xsd --output native_data.txt result.xml
    ```
4.  **Use as a Java Library**: Parse data programmatically within a Java application.
    ```java
    Compiler c = new Compiler();
    ProcessorFactory pf = c.compileFile(new File("my_schema.dfdl.xsd"));
    DataProcessor dp = pf.onPath("/");
    ParseResult res = dp.parse(new File("my_data.txt"));
    // Access parsed infoset from 'res'
    ```
5.  **Debug a Schema (CLI)**: Use the debugger to step through the parsing process.
    ```bash
    daffodil debug --schema my_schema.dfdl.xsd my_data.txt
    ```

## Apache DataFu

Apache DataFu is a collection of libraries for working with large-scale data in Apache Hadoop and Spark. It provides a rich set of well-tested User-Defined Functions (UDFs) for common data mining and statistical tasks. DataFu helps reduce boilerplate code and provides efficient implementations for tasks like sessionization, set operations, and sampling.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Raw Log Data] --> B{Spark DataFrame};
    B -- "Apply DataFu UDF" --> C["sessionize()"];
    C --> D[DataFrame with Session IDs];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "DataFu Libraries"
        A[datafu-spark.jar]
        B[datafu-pig.jar]
    end
    subgraph "Compute Engines"
        C[Apache Spark]
        D[Apache Pig (MapReduce)]
    end
    A -- "Provides UDFs for" --> C;
    B -- "Provides UDFs for" --> D;
```

### Examples (Spark/Scala)

1.  **Sessionization**: Group events into sessions based on a time window.
    ```scala
    import datafu.spark.functions._
    // Assume df has columns: userId, timestamp
    val sessionized = df.groupBy("userId").agg(sessionize(df("timestamp")).alias("sessions"))
    ```
2.  **Set Operations**: Perform a union on two sets within a DataFrame.
    ```scala
    // Assume df has columns: group, items (where items is an array)
    val combined = df.groupBy("group").agg(set_union(df("items")).alias("allItems"))
    ```
3.  **Simple Random Sampling**: Sample a fraction of rows from a DataFrame without replacement.
    ```scala
    val sampled = df.sample(false, 0.1) // Standard Spark, but DataFu provides more options
    ```
4.  **Median UDAF**: Calculate the median of a column (User-Defined Aggregation Function).
    ```scala
    // Register the UDAF first
    spark.udf.register("median", new Median())
    df.groupBy("category").agg(expr("median(value)"))
    ```
5.  **Assert UDF**: A utility for testing to ensure a condition is true for all rows.
    ```scala
    import datafu.spark.functions.ASSERT
    df.withColumn("check", ASSERT('colA > 0)).count() // Job fails if assertion is false
    ```

## Apache DataFusion

Apache DataFusion is an extensible query execution framework, written in Rust, that uses Apache Arrow as its in-memory format. It provides a high-performance, resource-efficient engine for running SQL queries against data in various formats like CSV and Parquet. DataFusion is designed to be embedded as a library within other applications to provide them with powerful analytical capabilities.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "DataFusion Engine"
        A[SQL Query] --> B{SQL Planner};
        B --> C[Logical Plan];
        C --> D{Physical Planner};
        D -- "Uses Arrow for in-memory format" --> E[Execution Engine];
    end
    subgraph "Data Sources"
        F[Parquet]
        G[CSV]
        H[Avro]
    end
    E -- "Reads from" --> F & G & H;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Python Application] -- "Uses" --> B[DataFusion Python Bindings];
    B -- "Talks to" --> C[Core DataFusion Engine (Rust)];
    C -- "Reads/Writes" --> D[Apache Arrow Memory Format];
```

### Examples (Python)

1.  **Create a Session Context**: The entry point for using DataFusion.
    ```python
    import datafusion

    ctx = datafusion.SessionContext()
    ```
2.  **Register a CSV as a Table**: Make a local CSV file queryable via SQL.
    ```python
    ctx.register_csv("my_table", "/path/to/data.csv")
    ```
3.  **Execute a SQL Query**: Run a standard SQL query against the registered table.
    ```python
    df = ctx.sql("SELECT a, b FROM my_table WHERE a > 10")
    ```
4.  **Collect Results**: Retrieve the results of the query as an Arrow Table.
    ```python
    arrow_table = df.collect()
    ```
5.  **Write to Parquet**: Save the results of a query to a Parquet file.
    ```python
    ctx.sql("COPY (SELECT * FROM my_table) TO '/path/to/output.parquet' (FORMAT 'parquet')")
    ```

## Apache DataSketches

Apache DataSketches is an open-source library of stochastic streaming algorithms, often called "sketches." These algorithms are used to approximate properties of massive datasets with high accuracy while using a fraction of the memory required by exact computations. DataSketches is ideal for large-scale monitoring systems, real-time analytics, and any application where approximate distinct counts, quantiles, or frequencies are acceptable.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Massive Data Stream] --> B{DataSketches Algorithm};
    subgraph "Inside the Sketch"
        B -- "Updates internal state" --> C[Compact, Fixed-Size Memory Representation];
    end
    C -- "Can be queried for" --> D[Approximate Result (e.g., distinct count)];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Use Case: Real-time Analytics"
        A[Event Stream (Kafka)] --> B{Spark Streaming};
        B -- "Updates Sketch per batch" --> C[ThetaSketch for Distinct Users];
        C -- "Periodically" --> D{Dashboard Server};
        D -- "Displays ~5.2M unique users" --> E[UI];
    end
```

### Examples (Spark/SQL)

1.  **Create a Theta Sketch for Distinct Counting**: Build a sketch to count unique user IDs.
    ```sql
    SELECT data_sketches_theta_sketch_build(userId) as user_sketch
    FROM events;
    ```
2.  **Get an Estimate from a Sketch**: Extract the approximate count from a single sketch.
    ```sql
    SELECT data_sketches_theta_sketch_get_estimate(user_sketch)
    FROM sketches_table;
    ```
3.  **Union Multiple Sketches**: Merge sketches from different time periods to get an overall distinct count.
    ```sql
    SELECT data_sketches_theta_sketch_get_estimate(
        data_sketches_theta_sketch_union(user_sketch)
    )
    FROM daily_sketches;
    ```
4.  **Create a KLL Quantiles Sketch**: Build a sketch to find the distribution of some value, like latency.
    ```sql
    SELECT data_sketches_kll_floats_sketch_build(latency_ms) as latency_sketch
    FROM performance_logs;
    ```
5.  **Get Quantiles from a Sketch**: Find the median (0.5), 95th, and 99th percentiles from the latency sketch.
    ```sql
    SELECT data_sketches_kll_floats_sketch_get_quantiles(latency_sketch, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99)
    FROM latency_sketches_table;
    ```

## Apache TVM

Apache TVM is an open-source machine learning compiler framework for CPUs, GPUs, and machine learning accelerators. It aims to close the gap between productivity-focused deep learning frameworks (like PyTorch and TensorFlow) and performance-oriented hardware backends. TVM compiles models from these high-level frameworks into optimized, low-level code for specific hardware targets.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "High-Level Frameworks"
        A[TensorFlow]
        B[PyTorch]
        C[ONNX]
    end
    subgraph "TVM Compiler Stack"
        D{Relay (High-Level IR)};
        E{Tensor Expression (Low-Level IR)};
        F{AutoTVM / AutoScheduler (Optimizers)};
        G[Code Generator];
    end
    subgraph "Hardware Targets"
        H[CPU (x86, ARM)]
        I[GPU (NVIDIA, AMD)]
        J[Accelerators (FPGA, etc.)]
    end
    A & B & C --> D;
    D --> E;
    E -- "Optimized by" --> F;
    F --> G;
    G --> H & I & J;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[PyTorch Model] -- "Import" --> B(TVM Relay Graph);
    B -- "Tune (AutoTVM)" --> C(Finds best schedule for target hardware);
    C -- "Compile" --> D[Optimized, Deployable Module];
    D -- "Run on" --> E{Target Device (e.g., GPU)};
```

### Examples (Python)

1.  **Import a Model**: Load a model from a framework like ONNX into TVM's high-level graph representation, Relay.
    ```python
    import onnx
    import tvm.relay as relay

    onnx_model = onnx.load("my_model.onnx")
    mod, params = relay.frontend.from_onnx(onnx_model)
    ```
2.  **Define a Target**: Specify the hardware you want to compile the model for.
    ```python
    target = tvm.target.Target("cuda", host="llvm")
    ```
3.  **Tune the Model (AutoTVM)**: Use TVM's auto-tuner to search for the most efficient low-level implementation for your specific hardware.
    ```python
    from tvm import autotvm

    tasks = autotvm.task.extract_from_program(mod["main"], target=target, params=params)
    for task in tasks:
        tuner.tune(task, ...) # This runs tuning trials
    ```
4.  **Compile the Model**: Build the final, optimized library using the tuning data.
    ```python
    with autotvm.apply_history_best(log_file):
        with tvm.transform.PassContext(opt_level=3):
            lib = relay.build(mod, target=target, params=params)
    ```
5.  **Run the Model**: Deploy the compiled module on the target hardware and perform inference.
    ```python
    from tvm.contrib import graph_executor

    dev = tvm.device(str(target), 0)
    module = graph_executor.GraphModule(lib["default"](dev))
    module.set_input("data", my_input_tensor)
    module.run()
    output = module.get_output(0)
    ```

## Apache Fluo

Apache Fluo is a distributed processing system that lets users make incremental updates to large data sets stored in Apache Accumulo. It is designed to expose the results of a large-scale computation as it is being updated, providing low-latency access to the latest results. This makes it ideal for use cases like updating search indexes, recalculating graph metrics, or maintaining materialized views where seeing fresh results quickly is critical. The core components are Observers, which are triggered by changes to data, and Transactions, which ensure data is updated atomically.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "External Systems"
        A[Data Ingest] --> B{Client Code};
        D[User Query] --> E{Client Code};
    end

    subgraph "Fluo Application"
        B -- "Writes to Accumulo via Fluo Transaction" --> C{Fluo};
        C -- Triggers --> F[Observer 1];
        C -- Triggers --> G[Observer 2];
        F -- "Makes derived updates" --> C;
    end

    subgraph "Storage Layer"
        C -- "Stores data and notifications" --> H[(Apache Accumulo)];
    end

    E -- "Reads latest results" --> C;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Transaction Start] --> B(Read row R, column C);
    B --> C{Check for Collision};
    C -- No Collision --> D(Write new value to R, C);
    D --> E(Set Notification for another Observer);
    E --> F[Commit];
    C -- Collision Detected --> G[Rollback & Retry];
```

### Examples (using Fluo API in Java)

1.  **Writing Data in a Transaction**: The basic unit of work in Fluo is a transaction. This example writes a name to a specific row and column.
    ```java
    // Assumes 'client' is a connected FluoClient
    try (Transaction tx = client.newTransaction()) {
      tx.set("r-001", new Column("meta", "name"), "John Doe");
      tx.commit();
    }
    ```
2.  **Creating an Observer**: An Observer is triggered when another transaction writes to a column it is configured to watch.
    ```java
    public class NameObserver extends AbstractObserver {
      @Override
      public void process(TransactionBase tx, Bytes row, Column col) throws Exception {
        // This code runs when meta:name is updated
        String name = tx.gets(row, col);
        tx.set(row, new Column("derived", "nameUpper"), name.toUpperCase());
      }

      @Override
      public ObservedColumn getObservedColumn() {
        return new ObservedColumn(new Column("meta", "name"), NotificationType.WEAK);
      }
    }
    ```
3.  **Configuring an Application**: You configure your application with observers and other settings before deploying it.
    ```java
    // In your main application setup
    FluoConfiguration config = new FluoConfiguration();
    config.setApplicationName("my-app");
    // ... set Accumulo connection properties ...
    config.addObserver(new ObserverSpecification(NameObserver.class.getName()));

    FluoFactory.newAdmin(config).initialize(
        new FluoAdmin.InitializationOptions().setClearZookeeper(true)
    );
    ```
4.  **Using a Fluo Recipe (Collision-Free Map)**: Fluo Recipes provide common patterns. This uses a map that avoids transaction collisions for concurrent updates.
    ```java
    // Assumes 'client' is a connected FluoClient
    CollisionFreeMap<String, Long> cfm = new CollisionFreeMap<>(
        "cfm-1", client, new StringEncoder(), new LongEncoder()
    );

    // Perform updates to map keys
    cfm.update("key1", 5L);
    cfm.update("key2", 10L);
    ```
5.  **Running Fluo on YARN**: The `fluo-yarn` command is used to deploy and manage a Fluo application on a YARN cluster.
    ```bash
    fluo-yarn start -c /path/to/fluo-conf
    ```

## Apache Airflow

Apache Airflow is a platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows. It represents workflows as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) of tasks, which are defined in Python scripts. This "workflows as code" approach makes them maintainable, versionable, testable, and collaborative, making Airflow a standard for complex data engineering pipelines.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Airflow Core Components"
        A[Web Server] -- "Presents UI" --> D{Metadata Database};
        B[Scheduler] -- "Triggers DAGs" --> D;
        C[Executor] -- "Runs Tasks" --> E[Workers];
    end
    D -- "Stores state of tasks/DAGs" --> B;
    B -- "Sends tasks to" --> C;
    subgraph "User-Defined"
        F[Python DAG File]
    end
    B -- "Parses" --> F;
```

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A(Start) --> B[Extract from API];
    A --> C[Wait for File in HDFS];
    B --> D{Transform Data with Spark};
    C --> D;
    D --> E[Load to Data Warehouse];
    E --> F(End);
```

### Examples (Python DAG Definitions)

1.  **Basic DAG Definition**: The boilerplate for creating a new workflow.
    ```python
    from airflow import DAG
    from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
    from datetime import datetime

    with DAG(
        dag_id='simple_bash_dag',
        start_date=datetime(2023, 1, 1),
        schedule_interval='@daily',
        catchup=False
    ) as dag:
        task1 = BashOperator(task_id='print_date', bash_command='date')
    ```
2.  **Defining Task Dependencies**: Setting the order in which tasks should run.
    ```python
    task1 = BashOperator(task_id='task_1', bash_command='echo "Task 1"')
    task2 = BashOperator(task_id='task_2', bash_command='echo "Task 2"')
    task3 = BashOperator(task_id='task_3', bash_command='echo "Task 3"')

    # Set dependencies: task1 must run before task2 and task3
    task1 >> [task2, task3]
    ```
3.  **Using the SparkSubmitOperator**: A task that submits a Spark job to the YARN cluster.
    ```python
    from airflow.providers.apache.spark.operators.spark_submit import SparkSubmitOperator

    spark_task = SparkSubmitOperator(
        task_id='spark_job',
        conn_id='spark_default', # Connection configured in Airflow UI
        application='/path/on/hdfs/to/my_spark_app.py',
        verbose=False
    )
    ```
4.  **Using a Sensor**: A task that waits for a condition to be met before continuing. This example waits for a file to appear in HDFS.
    ```python
    from airflow.providers.apache.hdfs.sensors.hdfs import HdfsSensor

    wait_for_file = HdfsSensor(
        task_id='wait_for_hdfs_file',
        hdfs_conn_id='hdfs_default',
        filepath='/user/data/landing/trigger_file.txt'
    )
    ```
5.  **Using Jinja Templating**: Passing dynamic information (like the execution date) into a task.
    ```python
    templated_command = """
    echo "Execution date is {{ ds }}"
    hdfs dfs -mkdir -p /user/data/processed/{{ ds }}
    """

    template_task = BashOperator(
        task_id='templated_task',
        bash_command=templated_command
    )
    ```

## Apache Knox

Apache Knox is an application gateway that provides a single point of secure access for REST APIs and UIs of Apache Hadoop services. It acts as a reverse proxy, hiding cluster details and simplifying client access by exposing a single endpoint for all services. Knox centralizes security by integrating with enterprise identity systems like LDAP and enforcing policies for authentication, authorization, and auditing.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "External World"
        Client -- "HTTPS Request" --> Knox;
    end
    subgraph "DMZ"
        Knox -- "Authenticates/Authorizes" --> IDM[Enterprise IDM / LDAP];
    end
    subgraph "Hadoop Cluster (Private Network)"
        Knox -- "Proxies Request (HTTP)" --> WebHDFS;
        Knox -- "Proxies Request (HTTP)" --> YARN_RM;
        Knox -- "Proxies Request (HTTP)" --> HBase_REST;
        Knox -- "Proxies Request (HTTP)" --> HiveServer2;
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Client Request<br/>/gateway/default/webhdfs/v1/] --> B{Knox Gateway};
    B -- "1. Authentication (e.g., LDAP)" --> C(Pass);
    C -- "2. Authorization (ACLs)" --> D(Pass);
    D -- "3. Dispatch to Service" --> E[WebHDFS Service Definition];
    E -- "4. Rewrite URL & Proxy" --> F[Internal HDFS NameNode<br/>:50070/webhdfs/v1/];
```

### Examples (Knox Topology Files)

1.  **Simplest Topology (`default.xml`)**: Exposing only WebHDFS.
    ```xml
    <topology>
        <gateway>
            <provider>
                <role>authentication</role>
                <name>ShiroProvider</name>
                <enabled>true</enabled>
                <param name="sessionTimeout" value="30"/>
                <param name="main.ldapRealm" value="org.apache.knox.gateway.realm.LdapRealm"/>
                <param name="main.ldapRealm.contextFactory.url" value="ldap://localhost:33389"/>
            </provider>
        </gateway>
        <service>
            <role>WEBHDFS</role>
            <url>http://namenode-host:50070/webhdfs</url>
        </service>
    </topology>
    ```
2.  **Accessing HDFS via Knox CLI**: Using Knox's proxy to list files.
    ```bash
    # Note the /gateway/default path prefix
    curl -iku "guest:guest-password" "https://knox-host:8443/gateway/default/webhdfs/v1/?op=LISTSTATUS"
    ```
3.  **Adding the YARN Service**: Extending the topology to include the YARN ResourceManager UI and API.
    ```xml
    <service>
        <role>RESOURCEMANAGER</role>
        <url>http://rm-host:8088/ws</url>
    </service>
    ```
4.  **Defining an ACL**: Creating an authorization rule to limit access to a service.
    ```xml
    <provider>
        <role>authorization</role>
        <name>AclsAuthz</name>
        <enabled>true</enabled>
        <param name="WEBHDFS.acl" value="admin;analyst;*;*"/>
    </provider>
    ```
5.  **Creating a Service-Level Topology**: A separate topology file for a specific use case, like exposing only Spark History.
    ```xml
    <topology>
        <gateway>
            </gateway>
        <service>
            <role>SPARKHISTORYUI</role>
            <url>http://spark-history-host:18080</url>
        </service>
    </topology>
    ```

## Apache Storm

Apache Storm is a free and open-source distributed real-time computation system. Storm makes it easy to reliably process unbounded streams of data, doing for real-time processing what Hadoop did for batch processing. It is simple, can be used with any programming language, and is known for its high speed, fault-tolerance, and guaranteed message processing. A Storm application, called a "topology," consists of "Spouts" (sources of streams) and "Bolts" (which process streams).

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Storm Cluster"
        A[Nimbus (Master)] -- "Distributes code & assigns tasks" --> B[ZooKeeper];
        C[Supervisors (Workers)] -- "Listen for tasks" --> B;
        C -- "Start/Stop" --> D[Worker Processes];
    end
    subgraph "User's Topology"
        E[Spout] -- "Emits tuples" --> F[Bolt 1];
        F -- "Emits tuples" --> G[Bolt 2];
    end
    D -- "Runs" --> E
    D -- "Runs" --> F
    D -- "Runs" --> G
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Kafka Topic] --> B(Kafka Spout);
    B -- "Raw Log Lines" --> C(Parse Bolt);
    C -- "Parsed Log Objects" --> D{Filter Bolt};
    D -- "Error Objects" --> E(Error Counting Bolt);
    E -- "Counts" --> F[Database];
    D -- "Other Objects" --> G(Ignore);
```

### Examples (in Java)

1.  **Creating a Spout**: A simple Spout that emits random words.
    ```java
    public class RandomWordSpout extends BaseRichSpout {
      private SpoutOutputCollector _collector;
      private Random _rand;

      @Override
      public void open(Map conf, TopologyContext context, SpoutOutputCollector collector) {
        _collector = collector;
        _rand = new Random();
      }

      @Override
      public void nextTuple() {
        String[] words = new String[]{"apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"};
        String word = words[_rand.nextInt(words.length)];
        _collector.emit(new Values(word));
      }

      @Override
      public void declareOutputFields(OutputFieldsDeclarer declarer) {
        declarer.declare(new Fields("word"));
      }
    }
    ```
2.  **Creating a Bolt**: A Bolt that appends "!!!" to each word it receives.
    ```java
    public class ExclamationBolt extends BaseRichBolt {
      private OutputCollector _collector;

      @Override
      public void prepare(Map conf, TopologyContext context, OutputCollector collector) {
        _collector = collector;
      }

      @Override
      public void execute(Tuple tuple) {
        _collector.emit(tuple, new Values(tuple.getString(0) + "!!!"));
        _collector.ack(tuple);
      }

      @Override
      public void declareOutputFields(OutputFieldsDeclarer declarer) {
        declarer.declare(new Fields("word-with-exclamation"));
      }
    }
    ```
3.  **Building the Topology**: Wiring the Spout and Bolt together.
    ```java
    TopologyBuilder builder = new TopologyBuilder();
    builder.setSpout("word_spout", new RandomWordSpout(), 5);
    builder.setBolt("exclaim_bolt", new ExclamationBolt(), 8).shuffleGrouping("word_spout");

    Config conf = new Config();
    conf.setDebug(true);
    ```
4.  **Submitting the Topology to a Cluster**: Packaging and deploying the topology.
    ```bash
    # Package the code into a JAR file: my-topology.jar
    storm jar my-topology.jar com.mycompany.MyTopology my-topology-name
    ```
5.  **Killing a Topology**: Stopping a running application on the cluster.
    ```bash
    storm kill my-topology-name
    ```

## Apache Phoenix

Apache Phoenix is an open-source, massively parallel, relational database engine that provides a SQL layer on top of Apache HBase. It allows you to interact with HBase data using standard JDBC and SQL, completely abstracting away the underlying NoSQL key-value store. Phoenix compiles SQL queries into native HBase scans, enabling low-latency analytical queries and operational workloads.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[User / Application] -- "JDBC / ODBC" --> B{Phoenix Query Engine};
    B -- "Standard SQL" --> C(SQL Parser & Optimizer);
    C -- "Compiles to" --> D[HBase Scans, Puts, Deletes];
    D -- "Executes on" --> E[(Apache HBase Cluster)];
    E -- "Stores data in HFiles on" --> F[(HDFS)];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Phoenix Table View"
        A["CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR, city VARCHAR)"]
    end
    subgraph "Underlying HBase Table View"
        B["Row Key: 1 --> Columns: 0:name='John', 0:city='NYC'"]
        C["Row Key: 2 --> Columns: 0:name='Jane', 0:city='SF'"]
    end
    A -- "Maps To" --> B & C
```

### Examples (Phoenix SQL via `sqlline.py`)

1.  **Create a Table**: Use standard SQL DDL to create a new table, which Phoenix maps to an HBase table.
    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE web_stats (
        host VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY,
        domain VARCHAR,
        feature VARCHAR,
        active_visitors BIGINT
    );
    ```
2.  **Upsert Data**: Use `UPSERT` (the equivalent of an insert/update) to add data.
    ```sql
    UPSERT INTO web_stats (host, domain, feature, active_visitors)
    VALUES ('www.example.com', 'example.com', 'login', 100);
    ```
3.  **Query Data**: Use standard `SELECT` statements to retrieve data with low latency.
    ```sql
    SELECT host, active_visitors FROM web_stats WHERE domain = 'example.com';
    ```
4.  **Create a Secondary Index**: To improve query performance on non-primary-key columns, you can create an index.
    ```sql
    CREATE INDEX idx_domain ON web_stats (domain) INCLUDE (active_visitors);
    ```
5.  **Delete Data**: Use standard `DELETE` statements to remove rows.
    ```sql
    DELETE FROM web_stats WHERE host = 'www.example.com';
    ```

## Apache Ranger

Apache Ranger provides centralized security administration for the Hadoop ecosystem. It allows you to define and enforce comprehensive, policy-based security for components like HDFS, Hive, HBase, and more. Ranger offers a central UI for managing policies and provides robust auditing capabilities to track all access attempts.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Admin] -- "Defines Policies" --> B[Ranger Admin UI];
    B -- "Stores Policies" --> C[(Policy Database)];
    subgraph "Hadoop Components"
        HDFS -- "Syncs Policies" --> C
        Hive -- "Syncs Policies" --> C
        HBase -- "Syncs Policies" --> C
    end
    subgraph "User Interaction"
        D[User] -- "Access Request (e.g., hdfs dfs -ls)" --> E{HDFS NameNode};
    end
    E -- "Intercepted by" --> F[Ranger HDFS Plugin];
    F -- "Enforces Policy" --> D;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Policy: Allow group 'analysts' to SELECT on table 'sales'] --> B{Ranger Policy DB};
    C[User 'alice' (in 'analysts' group)] -- "SELECT * FROM sales" --> D{HiveServer2};
    D -- "Is access allowed?" --> E[Ranger Hive Plugin];
    E -- "Checks policy from" --> B;
    E -- "Returns 'ALLOW'" --> D;
    D -- "Executes Query" --> C;
```

### Examples (Policy Definitions, described textually)

1.  **HDFS Policy for a Directory**: Create a policy that gives the `analysts` group read and execute access to the `/data/sales` directory in HDFS.
      * **Resource**: `path = /data/sales` (recursive)
      * **Allow Conditions**: `groups = analysts`, `permissions = Read, Execute`
      * **Deny Conditions**: (none)
2.  **Hive Policy for Column Masking**: Create a policy to protect PII. For the `users` table, allow the `support` group to see all columns, but for everyone else, show only the last 4 digits of the `ssn` column.
      * **Resource**: `database = default`, `table = users`, `column = ssn`
      * **Access Policy**: `groups = support`, `permissions = select`
      * **Masking Policy**: `groups = public`, `masking_type = MASK_SHOW_LAST_4`
3.  **Tag-Based Policy**: Create a policy based on data classification. Any table or column tagged with `PII` is denied access to the `external_contractors` group.
      * **Tag**: `PII`
      * **Deny Conditions**: `groups = external_contractors`
4.  **Row-Level Filter in Hive**: Create a policy that ensures users in the `us_sales` group can only see rows in the `transactions` table where the `country` column is 'USA'.
      * **Resource**: `database = default`, `table = transactions`
      * **Row Filter Policy**: `groups = us_sales`, `filter_expression = country = 'USA'`
5.  **Auditing Access**: View the Ranger audit logs to see that a user from a denied group attempted to access a protected HDFS directory and was rejected by the Ranger plugin.

## Apache Pinot

Apache Pinot is a real-time, distributed OLAP datastore designed to deliver scalable, low-latency analytics, even at high throughput. It is ideal for user-facing analytical applications, where users need to slice and dice large amounts of data interactively. Pinot achieves its speed through a columnar store, a variety of indexing techniques, and the ability to ingest data from both streaming sources (like Kafka) and batch sources (like HDFS).

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Data Ingestion"
        A[Streaming (Kafka)] --> B[Pinot Real-time Servers];
        C[Batch (HDFS)] --> D[Pinot Offline Servers];
    end
    subgraph "Query Path"
        E[User Query (PQL/SQL)] --> F{Pinot Broker};
        F -- "Scatter" --> B;
        F -- "Scatter" --> D;
        B --> G[Results];
        D --> G;
        G -- "Gather" --> F;
    end
    subgraph "Control Plane"
       H{Pinot Controller} -- "Manages Cluster" --> I[(ZooKeeper)];
       H -- "Manages" --> B & D & F;
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table WHERE country='US'] --> B{Broker};
    B -- "Forwards to all Servers with table segments" --> C[Server 1];
    B -- "Forwards to all Servers with table segments" --> D[Server 2];
    subgraph "Inside Server 1"
        C -- "Uses Inverted Index for 'country'" --> E(Finds matching document IDs);
        E -- "Scans only those documents" --> F(Partial Count);
    end
    F --> G{Broker};
    D --> G;
    G -- "Merges partial results" --> H[Final Count];
```

### Examples

1.  **Table Schema Definition (JSON)**: Define the columns and data types for a Pinot table.
    ```json
    {
      "schemaName": "metrics",
      "dimensionFieldSpecs": [
        {"name": "country", "dataType": "STRING"},
        {"name": "device", "dataType": "STRING"}
      ],
      "metricFieldSpecs": [
        {"name": "latencyMs", "dataType": "LONG"}
      ],
      "dateTimeFieldSpecs": [{
        "name": "ts", "dataType": "LONG",
        "format": "1:MILLISECONDS:EPOCH", "granularity": "1:MILLISECONDS"
      }]
    }
    ```
2.  **Table Config Definition (JSON)**: Define ingestion settings, replication, and indexing.
    ```json
    {
      "tableName": "metrics",
      "tableType": "REALTIME",
      "segmentsConfig": {
        "timeColumnName": "ts",
        "replication": "3"
      },
      "ingestionConfig": {
        "streamIngestionConfig": {
          "streamConfigMaps": [{"streamType": "kafka", "stream.kafka.consumer.type": "highLevel", "stream.kafka.topic.name": "metrics-topic", "stream.kafka.broker.list": "kafka:9092"}]
        }
      },
      "indexingConfig": {
        "invertedIndexColumns": ["country", "device"]
      }
    }
    ```
3.  **PQL Query - Simple Aggregation**: Count the total number of events.
    ```sql
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM metrics LIMIT 10
    ```
4.  **PQL Query - Group By**: Find the top 5 countries by number of events.
    ```sql
    SELECT country, COUNT(*) as eventCount
    FROM metrics
    GROUP BY country
    ORDER BY eventCount DESC
    LIMIT 5
    ```
5.  **PQL Query - Time-based Filtering**: Count events within the last 24 hours.
    ```sql
    SELECT COUNT(*)
    FROM metrics
    WHERE ts > now() - 86400000 -- (24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
    ```

## Apache Linkis

Apache Linkis is a computation middleware project that sits between upstream applications and downstream computation and storage engines. It provides a standardized set of REST/WebSocket APIs for submitting, managing, and monitoring jobs on various engines like Spark, Hive, and Flink. Linkis aims to decouple applications from the underlying engines, providing features like multi-tenant resource management, unified configuration, and job lifecycle control.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Upstream Tools / Applications"
        A[Web UI]
        B[Jupyter Notebook]
        C[Custom Application]
    end
    A & B & C -- "Standardized REST/WebSocket API" --> D{Linkis Gateway};

    subgraph "Linkis Services"
        D --> E[Entrance];
        E --> F[Orchestrator];
        F --> G[Engine Manager];
    end

    subgraph "Downstream Engines"
        G -- "Manages" --> H[Spark Engine];
        G -- "Manages" --> I[Hive Engine];
        G -- "Manages" --> J[Flink Engine];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    User --> App(Web App);
    App -- "1. Submit Code (Spark SQL)" --> Linkis;
    Linkis -- "2. Launch Spark Engine via YARN" --> YARN;
    YARN -- "3. Starts Spark" --> Spark(Spark Engine);
    Linkis -- "4. Sends code to Spark" --> Spark;
    Spark -- "5. Executes and returns result" --> Linkis;
    Linkis -- "6. Streams result back to App" --> App;
```

### Examples (API Calls and Configuration)

1.  **Submit a Spark SQL Job via REST API**:
    ```bash
    curl -X POST \
      http://linkis-gateway:9001/api/rest_j/v1/entrance/submit \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{
            "executionContent": {"code": "SHOW DATABASES", "runType": "sql"},
            "params": {"variable": {}, "configuration": {}},
            "labels": {"engineType": "spark-2.4.3", "userCreator": "hadoop-IDE"},
            "source": {"scriptPath": ""}
          }'
    ```
2.  **Get Job Status**: Use the task ID from the submission response to check on the job's progress.
    ```bash
    curl http://linkis-gateway:9001/api/rest_j/v1/entrance/exec_id/status
    ```
3.  **Get Job Logs**: Fetch the logs for a running or completed job.
    ```bash
    curl http://linkis-gateway:9001/api/rest_j/v1/entrance/exec_id/log
    ```
4.  **Kill a Job**: Terminate a running job via the API.
    ```bash
    curl -X POST \
      http://linkis-gateway:9001/api/rest_j/v1/entrance/exec_id/kill \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    ```
5.  **Engine Configuration**: An administrator can configure engine properties, like Spark driver memory, within the Linkis management console, and these settings will be applied to all jobs submitted by users. This centralizes resource management.

## Apache Kibble

Apache Kibble is a suite of tools for collecting, aggregating, and visualizing activity in software projects and communities. It scans various sources like source code repositories (Git), mailing lists, and issue trackers to build a comprehensive picture of project health and contributor activity. Kibble is primarily a data platform and visualization tool used by open-source foundations and communities to understand their projects better.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph Data Sources
        A[Git Repositories]
        B[Mailing Lists]
        C[Issue Trackers]
        D[Forums]
    end
    subgraph Kibble Platform
        E{Kibble Scanner};
        F[Elasticsearch (Storage)];
        G[Kibble Web UI];
    end
    A & B & C & D --> E;
    E -- "Stores parsed data" --> F;
    G -- "Queries and Visualizes" --> F;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Scan Phase"
        Scanner -- "git clone" --> Git;
        Scanner -- "Fetch Archives" --> MailingList;
    end
    subgraph "Analysis Phase"
        Scanner -- "Analyze Commits & Emails" --> A{Identify People & Organizations};
        A --> B{Generate Stats};
    end
    subgraph "Storage/UI"
        B --> C[Store in Elasticsearch];
        C --> D[Visualize in Web UI];
    end
```

### Examples (Configuration and Usage)

1.  **Basic Source Configuration (`kibble.yml`)**: Telling Kibble which organization to scan.
    ```yaml
    kibble:
      name: "Apache Software Foundation"
      organisation: "ASF"
      scanners:
        - git
        - mail
      sources:
        asf-git:
          type: git
          sourceID: asf-git
          location: "https://gitbox.apache.org/repos/asf"
        asf-ponymail:
          type: ponymail
          sourceID: asf-ponymail
          location: "https://lists.apache.org"
    ```
2.  **Running a Scan**: Invoking the Kibble scanner from the command line.
    ```bash
    ./kibble.py scan --source asf-git
    ```
3.  **Viewing Project Commits**: Interacting with the Kibble web UI to see a timeline of commits for a specific project. This is a user action, not code.
4.  **Querying via API**: Kibble exposes an API. This example fetches statistics for a mailing list.
    ```bash
    curl "http://kibble-server/api/stats?sourceID=asf-ponymail&list=dev@project.apache.org"
    ```
5.  **Defining a View**: Configuring a "view" in `kibble.yml` to group multiple repositories and mailing lists into a single logical project.
    ```yaml
    views:
      - name: "Apache HTTPD"
        sourceID: asf-httpd-view
        repos:
          - httpd.git
          - httpd-docs.git
        lists:
          - dev@httpd.apache.org
          - user@httpd.apache.org
    ```

## Apache Arrow

Apache Arrow provides a standardized, language-independent columnar memory format for flat and hierarchical data, organized for efficient analytic operations on modern hardware. It is designed to accelerate in-memory data processing and interchange between systems without the overhead of serialization and deserialization. By providing a common data representation, Arrow enables high-performance data transport and analytics across a wide range of tools and languages.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Traditional Data Interchange"
        A[System 1 (e.g., Spark)] -- Serialize --> B(Data on Disk/Network);
        B -- Deserialize --> C[System 2 (e.g., Pandas)];
    end
    subgraph "Arrow-based Interchange"
        D[System 1] -- "Writes to Arrow format" --> E(Shared Arrow Buffer);
        E -- "Zero-copy read" --> F[System 2];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Arrow Memory Layout"
        A[Column] --> B(Validity Bitmap);
        A --> C(Data Buffer);
        A --> D(Offset Buffer for variable-size types);
    end
```

### Examples (Python/PyArrow)

1.  **Creating an Arrow Array**: The fundamental data structure for a single column.
    ```python
    import pyarrow as pa

    # Create an array of 32-bit integers
    array = pa.array([1, 2, 3, 4], type=pa.int32())
    ```
2.  **Creating a RecordBatch**: A collection of arrays of the same length, representing a chunk of a table.
    ```python
    batch = pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays(
        [pa.array([1, 2, 3]), pa.array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'])],
        names=['numbers', 'strings']
    )
    ```
3.  **Converting Pandas DataFrame to Arrow Table**: A common use case for efficient data exchange.
    ```python
    import pandas as pd

    df = pd.DataFrame({'int': [1, 2], 'str': ['a', 'b']})
    table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df)
    ```
4.  **Writing an Arrow Table to a File**: Using the Feather format, a fast on-disk representation of Arrow data.
    ```python
    with pa.OSFile('data.arrow', 'wb') as sink:
        with pa.ipc.new_file(sink, table.schema) as writer:
            writer.write_table(table)
    ```
5.  **Inter-process Communication (IPC)**: Sending Arrow data between processes with zero-copy reads.
    ```python
    # In one process (writer)
    buf = pa.serialize(table).to_buffer()

    # In another process (reader)
    restored_table = pa.deserialize(buf)
    ```

## Apache Helix

Apache Helix is a generic cluster management framework used for the automatic management of partitioned, replicated, and distributed resources. It simplifies the process of building distributed systems by providing common functionalities like fault tolerance, automated rebalancing, and state management. Helix uses ZooKeeper to maintain the state of the cluster, including which nodes are live and how resources are partitioned among them.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Cluster Operator] -- "Defines Ideal State" --> B[(ZooKeeper)];
    C[Controller] -- "Observes" --> B;
    C -- "Calculates and sends state transitions" --> D[Participants (Nodes)];
    D -- "Updates Current State" --> B;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Resource: myDatabase (3 partitions, 2 replicas)"
        P1[Partition 1]
        P2[Partition 2]
        P3[Partition 3]
    end
    subgraph "Node A"
        P1_Master("P1 (Master)")
        P2_Slave("P2 (Slave)")
    end
    subgraph "Node B"
        P2_Master("P2 (Master)")
        P3_Slave("P3 (Slave)")
    end
    subgraph "Node C"
        P3_Master("P3 (Master)")
        P1_Slave("P1 (Slave)")
    end
```

### Examples (Helix Admin CLI)

1.  **Add a New Cluster**: Define a new cluster to be managed by Helix.
    ```bash
    /opt/helix/bin/helix-admin.sh --zkSvr localhost:2181 --addCluster my-database-cluster
    ```
2.  **Add a Node**: Register a new node that will host resources for the cluster.
    ```bash
    /opt/helix/bin/helix-admin.sh --zkSvr localhost:2181 --addNode my-database-cluster --node server-1:1234
    ```
3.  **Add a Resource**: Define a new distributed resource, like a database with multiple partitions.
    ```bash
    /opt/helix/bin/helix-admin.sh --zkSvr localhost:2181 --addResource my-database-cluster --resource my_db --partitions 16 --stateModel MasterSlave
    ```
4.  **Rebalance a Resource**: Tell Helix to automatically distribute the partitions of the resource among the available nodes.
    ```bash
    /opt/helix/bin/helix-admin.sh --zkSvr localhost:2181 --rebalance my-database-cluster --resource my_db --replicas 3
    ```
5.  **Enable/Disable a Node**: Temporarily take a node offline for maintenance without causing data loss.
    ```bash
    /opt/helix/bin/helix-admin.sh --zkSvr localhost:2181 --enableInstance my-database-cluster --node server-1:1234 --enable false
    ```

## Apache Hop

Apache Hop is a visual data integration platform designed to be easy to use, extensible, and capable of handling a wide variety of data engineering tasks. It allows users to build complex data pipelines using a graphical interface, reducing the need for custom coding. Hop can run these pipelines on its own engine or orchestrate their execution on distributed compute engines like Apache Spark.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Hop Design Environment"
        A[Hop GUI] --> B{Pipeline/Workflow Metadata};
    end
    subgraph "Execution"
        B -- "Can be run by" --> C[Local Hop Engine];
        B -- "Can be run by" --> D[Remote Hop Server];
        B -- "Can be orchestrated on" --> E[Spark/Flink];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[CSV Input] --> B{Select Values};
    B --> C{Filter Rows};
    C --> D[Database Lookup];
    D --> E[Table Output];
```

### Examples

1.  **Run a Workflow (CLI)**: Execute a Hop workflow file from the command line.
    ```bash
    /opt/hop/hop-run.sh -w /path/to/my-workflow.hwf
    ```
2.  **Passing Parameters to a Pipeline**: Supply dynamic values to a pipeline at runtime.
    ```bash
    /opt/hop/hop-run.sh -p /path/to/my-pipeline.hpl -a INPUT_DIR=/data/landing -a OUTPUT_DIR=/data/processed
    ```
3.  **Using Hop Server**: Start the Hop server to allow remote execution of pipelines.
    ```bash
    /opt/hop/hop-server.sh /path/to/server-config.xml
    ```
4.  **Exporting Metadata**: Export all project metadata to a JSON file for version control.
    ```bash
    /opt/hop/hop-conf.sh --export-to-json=/path/to/metadata.json
    ```
5.  **Connecting to Hadoop**: In the Hop GUI, create a new "Hadoop Cluster" connection by pointing it to the location of your `core-site.xml` and `hdfs-site.xml` files to enable HDFS file access.

## Apache Iceberg

Apache Iceberg is an open table format for huge analytic datasets, designed to improve on the reliability and performance of traditional Hive tables. It provides features like ACID transactions, schema evolution, and hidden partitioning, all while allowing multiple compute engines to work on the same data concurrently. Iceberg is not a service but a library that manages table metadata.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Compute Engines"
        A[Spark]
        B[Flink]
        C[Trino]
    end
    subgraph "Iceberg Table"
        D{Metadata Pointer};
        E[Manifest List];
        F[Manifest File];
        G[Data File (Parquet/ORC)];
    end
    A & B & C -- "Read/Write via" --> D;
    D -- "Points to" --> E;
    E -- "Lists" --> F;
    F -- "Tracks" --> G;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[v1 metadata.json] -- "Transaction 1: Add data" --> B[v2 metadata.json];
    B -- "Transaction 2: Delete data" --> C[v3 metadata.json];
    D[Query Engine] -- "Reads latest" --> C;
    E[Time-travel Query] -- "Reads previous version" --> B;
```

### Examples (Spark SQL)

1.  **Create an Iceberg Table**: Define a partitioned Iceberg table.
    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE my_iceberg_table (
        id BIGINT,
        category STRING,
        ts TIMESTAMP
    )
    USING iceberg
    PARTITIONED BY (days(ts), category);
    ```
2.  **Insert Data**: Add new rows to the table. This is an atomic operation.
    ```sql
    INSERT INTO my_iceberg_table VALUES (1, 'A', '2023-10-27 10:00:00');
    ```
3.  **Schema Evolution (Add a Column)**: Safely add a new column without rewriting old data.
    ```sql
    ALTER TABLE my_iceberg_table ADD COLUMN new_col STRING;
    ```
4.  **Time Travel Query**: Query the table as it existed at a specific point in time.
    ```sql
    -- Using a timestamp
    SELECT * FROM my_iceberg_table TIMESTAMP AS OF '2023-10-26 00:00:00';

    -- Using a snapshot ID
    SELECT * FROM my_iceberg_table VERSION AS OF 1234567890123456789;
    ```
5.  **Optimize a Table**: Compact small data files into larger ones to improve query performance.
    ```sql
    CALL hadoop_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'my_iceberg_table');
    ```

## Apache InLong

Apache InLong is a one-stop, full-lifecycle data integration and synchronization platform for massive data. It provides automatic, safe, and reliable data transmission capabilities, supporting both batch and streaming data. InLong simplifies the process of building data pipelines by integrating components for collection, aggregation, caching, and sinking data to various storage systems.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Data Sources] --> B{InLong Agent/SDK};
    B --> C[DataProxy (Cache)];
    C --> D[TubeMQ (Message Queue)];
    D --> E{InLong Sort};
    E -- "Writes to" --> F[Data Sinks (HDFS, Hive, etc.)];
    G[InLong Manager] -- "Manages all components" --> B & C & D & E;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Data Flow"
        A[Log File] -- "Agent collects" --> B(DataProxy);
        B -- "Forwards to" --> C(TubeMQ);
        C -- "Consumed by" --> D(Sort);
        D -- "Writes to" --> E[(HDFS)];
    end
```

### Examples

1.  **Create a Data Stream (UI)**: In the InLong Manager UI, define a new data stream, specifying the source type (e.g., file), and the sink type (e.g., Hive).
2.  **Configure an Agent (agent.json)**: Configure a local agent to collect data from a file and send it to the DataProxy.
    ```json
    {
      "job": { "id": 1, "name": "file_collection_job" },
      "source": { "type": "TextFileSource", "pattern": "/var/log/app/.*.log" },
      "sink": { "type": "ProxySink", "proxy.inlong.group.id": "my_stream_id" }
    }
    ```
3.  **Query Data in Hive**: Once the data flows through the pipeline, query the target Hive table that InLong created and manages.
    ```sql
    SELECT * FROM my_stream_id_table LIMIT 10;
    ```
4.  **Check Stream Status (UI)**: Use the Manager UI to monitor the real-time data flow rate, number of messages, and status of each component in the stream.
5.  **Start Standalone Cluster**: For testing, start all InLong components with a single command.
    ```bash
    /opt/inlong/bin/inlong-standalone.sh start
    ```

## Apache Kudu

Apache Kudu is a columnar storage engine for structured data that supports both fast analytics and low-latency random access. It is designed to enable hybrid transactional/analytical processing (HTAP) by combining the advantages of columnar formats with the ability to perform rapid updates and inserts. Kudu integrates with the Hadoop ecosystem, particularly with Apache Impala and Spark, to provide a powerful engine for real-time analytics.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Kudu Master] -- "Manages metadata" --> B[(Catalog Table)];
    A -- "Manages" --> C[Tablet Servers];
    subgraph "Tablet Server"
        D[Tablet 1]
        E[Tablet 2]
    end
    C --> D & E;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Data] -- "Written via" --> B{Kudu Client};
    B -- "Writes to" --> C[Tablet Server];
    subgraph "Inside Tablet Server"
        C --> D{In-memory RowSet (Deltas)};
        D -- "Flushed to" --> E[On-disk Columnar RowSet];
    end
```

### Examples (Kudu CLI and Spark)

1.  **Create a Table (CLI)**: Use the Kudu CLI to define a new table with a primary key and partitioning scheme.
    ```bash
    kudu table create 'my-master-host' 'my_first_table' \
    '("id" int32, "name" string, PRIMARY KEY ("id"))' \
    --num_replicas 3
    ```
2.  **Insert Data (Spark)**: Use the Kudu Spark integration to write a DataFrame to a Kudu table.
    ```python
    df.write.format('kudu') \
      .option('kudu.master', 'my-master-host:7051') \
      .option('kudu.table', 'my_first_table') \
      .mode('append').save()
    ```
3.  **Upsert Data (Spark)**: Update existing rows or insert new ones.
    ```python
    df_updates.write.format('kudu') \
      .option('kudu.master', 'my-master-host:7051') \
      .option('kudu.table', 'my_first_table') \
      .mode('append').option('kudu.operation', 'upsert').save()
    ```
4.  **Query Data (Spark)**: Read data from a Kudu table into a Spark DataFrame.
    ```python
    kudu_df = spark.read.format('kudu') \
      .option('kudu.master', 'my-master-host:7051') \
      .option('kudu.table', 'my_first_table').load()
    ```
5.  **Check Cluster Health (CLI)**: Get a report on the status of the Kudu masters and tablet servers.
    ```bash
    kudu cluster ksck my-master-host
    ```

## Apache Kylin

Apache Kylin is an open-source, distributed Analytical Data Warehouse for Big Data that provides an OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) engine. It pre-calculates and stores multidimensional data "cubes" on HDFS, allowing for near-constant query time regardless of the size of the underlying dataset. Kylin is designed to provide sub-second query latency for SQL queries against petabyte-scale data by avoiding on-the-fly computation.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Hive Tables] -- "Data Source" --> B{Kylin Cube};
    B -- "Builds on" --> C[Hadoop/Spark];
    B -- "Stores Cube in" --> D[(HDFS)];
    E[BI Tool / SQL Client] -- "SQL Query" --> F{Kylin Query Engine};
    F -- "Reads pre-aggregated data from" --> D;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Build Phase"
        A[Hive Fact & Dimension Tables] --> B{Kylin builds Cuboids};
        B -- "Each Cuboid is a pre-aggregated view" --> C[(HBase/HDFS)];
    end
    subgraph "Query Phase"
        D[SQL Query] --> E{Kylin identifies smallest Cuboid};
        E -- "Scans only that Cuboid" --> F[Result];
    end
```

### Examples

1.  **Define a Data Model (UI)**: In the Kylin UI, create a data model by selecting a fact table and its corresponding dimension tables from Hive.
2.  **Design a Cube (UI)**: Based on the data model, design a cube by choosing which columns will be dimensions (for grouping) and which will be measures (for aggregation).
3.  **Build a Cube (UI/API)**: Trigger a build job for a segment of the cube (e.g., one day of data). Kylin will launch a MapReduce or Spark job to process the raw data and generate the cube.
    ```bash
    # Example API call to trigger a build
    curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Basic ..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    http://kylin-host:7070/kylin/api/cubes/my_cube/build \
    -d '{"startTime": 1666828800000, "endTime": 1666915200000, "buildType": "BUILD"}'
    ```
4.  **Query via SQL**: Connect a BI tool or SQL client to Kylin's JDBC endpoint and run a standard SQL query. Kylin will answer it by reading the pre-aggregated data from the cube instead of scanning the raw Hive tables.
    ```sql
    SELECT country, SUM(price)
    FROM sales_fact
    JOIN country_dim ON sales_fact.country_id = country_dim.id
    GROUP BY country;
    ```
5.  **Check Cube Status (UI)**: Monitor the size, build progress, and query statistics of your cubes from the Kylin web interface.

## Apache ORC

Apache ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) is a free and open-source columnar storage format for data in the Hadoop ecosystem. It is designed for high-performance reading, writing, and processing of large datasets by using techniques like compression, predicate pushdown, and lightweight indexing. Because it is a library and not a service, its "deployment" means it is included and used by data processing engines like Spark and Hive.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Table Data] --> B{ORC Writer};
    subgraph "ORC File Structure"
        B --> C[File Footer];
        C --> D[Stripe 1];
        C --> E[Stripe 2];
        D --> F[Index Data];
        D --> G[Row Data (Columnar)];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[SQL Query: SELECT col1 FROM table WHERE col2 = 'X'] --> B{ORC Reader};
    B -- "1. Read File Footer" --> C(Get file-level stats);
    B -- "2. Read Stripe Footers" --> D(Get stripe-level stats);
    D -- "3. Skip stripes where col2 cannot be 'X'" --> E[Read only relevant stripes];
    E -- "4. Read only col1 data" --> F[Result];
```

### Examples (Spark SQL)

1.  **Create an ORC Table**: Define a new table and specify ORC as the storage format.
    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE my_orc_table (id INT, value STRING) STORED AS ORC;
    ```
2.  **Write Data to an ORC Table**: Insert data into the table. Spark will use the ORC writer library.
    ```sql
    INSERT INTO my_orc_table SELECT id, value FROM source_table;
    ```
3.  **Read Data from an ORC Table**: Querying the table is transparent; Spark's engine will leverage ORC's features automatically.
    ```sql
    SELECT * FROM my_orc_table WHERE id > 100;
    ```
4.  **Specify Compression**: Choose a compression codec when writing data to save space.
    ```python
    # In PySpark
    df.write.format("orc") \
      .option("compression", "zlib") \
      .save("hdfs:///path/to/output")
    ```
5.  **Inspect ORC File Metadata**: Use the `orc-tools` command-line utility to view the internal structure of an ORC file.
    ```bash
    java -jar orc-tools-*.jar meta /path/on/hdfs/to/file.orc
    ```

## Apache Ozone

Apache Ozone is a scalable, redundant, and distributed object store for Hadoop. It is designed to handle both small and large files efficiently, overcoming some of the limitations of HDFS, particularly for environments with billions of small objects. Ozone provides an S3-compatible interface, making it a modern alternative for data storage in the Hadoop ecosystem.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Client] -- "S3/RPC Request" --> B{Ozone Manager (OM)};
    B -- "Manages metadata namespace" --> C{Storage Container Manager (SCM)};
    C -- "Manages blocks & replication" --> D[DataNodes];
    Client -- "Reads/Writes data blocks" --> D;
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    subgraph "Ozone Namespace"
        A[Volume] --> B[Bucket];
        B --> C[Key (Object)];
    end
    subgraph "Physical Storage"
        C -- "Is broken into" --> D[Blocks];
        D -- "Are stored in" --> E[Containers];
        E -- "Replicated across" --> F[(DataNodes)];
    end
```

### Examples (Ozone CLI)

1.  **Create a Volume**: The top-level container for buckets, similar to a user's home directory.
    ```bash
    ozone sh volume create /my-volume
    ```
2.  **Create a Bucket**: A container for objects (keys), similar to a directory.
    ```bash
    ozone sh bucket create /my-volume/my-bucket
    ```
3.  **Put a Key (Upload a File)**: Upload a local file into a bucket.
    ```bash
    ozone sh key put /my-volume/my-bucket/my-file.txt /local/path/to/file.txt
    ```
4.  **Get a Key (Download a File)**: Download an object from a bucket to a local file.
    ```bash
    ozone sh key get /my-volume/my-bucket/my-file.txt /local/path/to/downloaded_file.txt
    ```
5.  **List Keys in a Bucket**: List all the objects stored within a bucket.
    ```bash
    ozone sh key list /my-volume/my-bucket
    ```

## Apache Parquet

Apache Parquet is a highly efficient, open-source columnar storage format for data in the Hadoop ecosystem. It is designed for performance, using advanced compression and encoding schemes to minimize storage space and accelerate analytical queries. Parquet is a library, not a service, and is the default storage format for many data processing frameworks like Apache Spark.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Row-based Data] --> B{Parquet Writer};
    subgraph "Parquet File Structure"
        B --> C[File Footer (Metadata)];
        C --> D[Row Group 1];
        C --> E[Row Group 2];
        D --> F[Column Chunk (Col A)];
        D --> G[Column Chunk (Col B)];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Query: SELECT col_B FROM table WHERE col_A = 5] --> B{Parquet Reader};
    B -- "1. Read Footer for schema & stats" --> C(Read Metadata);
    C -- "2. Use Row Group stats to skip groups" --> D[Read only relevant Row Groups];
    D -- "3. Read only Column Chunk for col_B" --> E[Result];
```

### Examples (Spark SQL and PySpark)

1.  **Writing a DataFrame to Parquet**: This is the default behavior in Spark.
    ```python
    # In PySpark
    df.write.save("hdfs:///path/to/my_data.parquet")
    ```
2.  **Reading a Parquet File**: Spark automatically infers the schema from the Parquet metadata.
    ```python
    parquet_df = spark.read.parquet("hdfs:///path/to/my_data.parquet")
    ```
3.  **Creating a Parquet-backed Table**: Define an external table in Hive or Spark that points to Parquet data.
    ```sql
    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE my_parquet_table (id INT, value STRING)
    STORED AS PARQUET
    LOCATION '/path/to/my_data.parquet';
    ```
4.  **Predicate Pushdown**: This happens automatically. The query below will only read row groups where `category` could possibly be 'A', significantly reducing I/O.
    ```sql
    SELECT * FROM my_parquet_table WHERE category = 'A';
    ```
5.  **Inspecting Parquet Metadata**: Use the `parquet-tools` utility to view the file's internal structure, including schema and row group statistics.
    ```bash
    java -jar parquet-tools-*.jar meta /path/on/hdfs/to/file.parquet
    ```

## Apache Pulsar

Apache Pulsar is a distributed, open-source pub-sub messaging and streaming platform built for scalability, performance, and reliability. It combines high-throughput messaging with a stream storage layer, provided by Apache BookKeeper, to offer features like guaranteed message delivery and topic retention. Pulsar's multi-tenant architecture and tiered storage make it well-suited for large-scale enterprise use cases.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Pulsar Cluster"
        A[Producers] --> B{Brokers};
        C[Consumers] --> B;
        B -- "Read/Write Ledger Data" --> D[Bookies (BookKeeper)];
    end
    subgraph "Coordination"
        B & D -- "Use for metadata" --> E[(ZooKeeper)];
    end
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Producer] -- "Sends message" --> B(Broker);
    B -- "Writes to multiple Bookies" --> C[Bookie 1];
    B -- "Writes to multiple Bookies" --> D[Bookie 2];
    B -- "Writes to multiple Bookies" --> E[Bookie 3];
    C & D & E -- "Ack to Broker" --> B;
    B -- "Ack to Producer" --> A;
```

### Examples (Pulsar Client CLI)

1.  **Produce a Message**: Send a simple message to a topic.
    ```bash
    /opt/pulsar/bin/pulsar-client produce persistent://public/default/my-topic \
      -m "Hello, Pulsar!" -n 1
    ```
2.  **Consume Messages**: Create a subscription and consume messages from a topic.
    ```bash
    /opt/pulsar/bin/pulsar-client consume persistent://public/default/my-topic \
      -s "my-subscription" -n 10
    ```
3.  **Create a Partitioned Topic**: Create a topic with multiple partitions to increase throughput.
    ```bash
    /opt/pulsar/bin/pulsar-admin topics create-partitioned-topic \
      persistent://public/default/my-partitioned-topic --partitions 4
    ```
4.  **Check Topic Stats**: Get statistics for a topic, including message rates and storage size.
    ```bash
    /opt/pulsar/bin/pulsar-admin topics stats persistent://public/default/my-topic
    ```
5.  **Create a Tenant**: In a multi-tenant setup, create a new tenant to isolate resources.
    ```bash
    /opt/pulsar/bin/pulsar-admin tenants create my-tenant --admin-roles my-admin-role
    ```

## Apache Samza

Apache Samza is a distributed stream processing framework that uses Apache Kafka for messaging and Apache YARN for resource management and fault tolerance. It allows you to write stateful applications that process data in near real-time, with strong guarantees for durability and ordering. Samza is designed to be simple to operate and scales horizontally by adding more containers on the YARN cluster.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A[Input Kafka Topic] --> B{Samza Job};
    B -- "Runs on" --> C[YARN Container];
    B -- "Writes to" --> D[Output Kafka Topic];
    B -- "Stores state in" --> E[RocksDB (on local disk)];
    E -- "Backed up to" --> F[Changelog Kafka Topic];
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[YARN ApplicationMaster] -- "Requests containers" --> B(YARN ResourceManager);
    B -- "Allocates" --> C[NodeManager];
    C -- "Launches" --> D[Samza Container];
    subgraph "Inside Samza Container"
        D --> E(Task Instance);
        E -- "Reads from" --> F[Kafka Partition];
        E -- "Writes to" --> G[Local State Store];
    end
```

### Examples (Job Configuration Properties)

1.  **Defining a Job**: Basic configuration for a Samza job.
    ```properties
    job.name=my-samza-job
    job.factory.class=org.apache.samza.job.yarn.YarnJobFactory
    ```
2.  **Defining Input and Output Streams**: Specifying the Kafka topics for the job.
    ```properties
    task.inputs=kafka.my-input-topic
    systems.kafka.streams.my-output-topic.samza.msg.serde=string
    ```
3.  **Configuring the Kafka System**: Telling Samza how to connect to Kafka.
    ```properties
    systems.kafka.samza.factory=org.apache.samza.system.kafka.KafkaSystemFactory
    systems.kafka.consumer.zookeeper.connect=zookeeper-quorum:2181/
    systems.kafka.producer.bootstrap.servers=kafka-brokers:9092
    ```
4.  **Configuring State Storage**: Setting up RocksDB for durable local state.
